rp-skill.when: When you have an established practice and want to formalize it.
rp-skill.impact: Without a template the Skill often «doesn't trigger» because of a bad trigger.
rp-skill.mistakes: Not specifying triggers explicitly — the Skill won't activate when needed.

rp-claudemd.title: Create CLAUDE.md
rp-claudemd.what: A prompt to generate CLAUDE.md with the right structure: stack, conventions, taboos, entry points.
rp-claudemd.why: A ready project file in 1 minute — not an hour of manual formatting.
rp-claudemd.when: In every project where you run Claude Code.
rp-claudemd.impact: CLAUDE.md from a template = the model writes code «in project style» right away.
rp-claudemd.mistakes: Not specifying taboos — Claude will use patterns forbidden in the project.

rp-audit.title: Expert audit
rp-audit.what: A prompt checklist: structure, clarity, risks, principle alignment, final recommendation.
rp-audit.why: Covers 80% of typical issues in one pass.
rp-audit.when: Before launching something new or after a major change.
rp-audit.impact: A structured audit = actions instead of opinions.
rp-audit.mistakes: Not specifying context and audience — recommendations will be detached from reality.

scenarios.title: Use cases
scenarios.what: Typical tasks where Claude delivers max value: code, design, content, research, analysis.
scenarios.why: So you see where to apply the tool right away — without long «where will it help me?».
scenarios.when: At the start of Claude work — define 1-2 of your scenarios and deepen them.
scenarios.impact: Understanding the scenario → choosing the right tool (Project / Skill / Code / Artifact).
scenarios.example: I have a regular task — <describe>. What scenario and tool stack is optimal?
scenarios.mistakes: Using Claude everywhere «a little bit» — nowhere will you get to expert level.

sc-analysis.title: Analysis and audit
sc-analysis.what: Expert audit, code review, document audit, security review.
sc-analysis.why: Claude is strongest where deep analysis and weighed conclusions are needed.
sc-analysis.when: When you have an artifact (page, code, document) and need conclusions.
sc-analysis.impact: A good prompt + Project = an audit at a competent expert's level in minutes.
sc-analysis.example: Run an audit of this material against a clear set of criteria (structure, clarity, risks).
sc-analysis.mistakes: Asking «give an evaluation» without criteria — you'll get generic phrases.

sc-coding.title: Programming
sc-coding.what: Code writing, refactoring, debugging, migrations, tests — especially in Claude Code.
sc-coding.why: Claude is one of the best coding models; combined with the CLI it becomes almost an intern.
sc-coding.when: Any development from prototype to production.
sc-coding.impact: Works stronger with CLAUDE.md and Hooks — otherwise it drifts into its own habits.
sc-coding.example: Rewrite this endpoint so it uses transactions and caches the result for 60s.
sc-coding.mistakes: Working in chat, not in Claude Code — you lose file and history access.

sc-design.title: Design and UX
sc-design.what: Prototypes, UX copy, design critique, accessibility audit — especially with Figma MCP.
sc-design.why: Claude sees the design, understands context, suggests options — at the level of a competent expert.
sc-design.when: Any task from research to handoff — there are ready-made Skills (design:*).
sc-design.impact: When Claude sees the system itself via MCP — work quality with it rises especially sharply.
sc-design.example: Open this layout, do a design critique and propose 3 improvements to the hero section.
sc-design.mistakes: Doing design «through text» without screenshots and real mockups — you lose half the context.

sc-content.title: Content
sc-content.what: Long-reads, social posts, email, documentation, translations.
sc-content.why: Claude is good at sensing tone, brand voice — especially with examples.
sc-content.when: When you need text you wouldn't be embarrassed to publish.
sc-content.impact: With a Project and a brand guide — you get texts «in voice» without editing.
sc-content.example: Write a 1500-word longread about IT burnout — in our tone (examples above).
sc-content.mistakes: Asking to «write a post» without audience and tone — you'll get generic output.

sc-research.title: Research
sc-research.what: Analysis of articles, competitors, market, synthesis of interviews, literature reviews.
sc-research.why: Claude is good at synthesis — extract patterns from 50 sources in minutes.
sc-research.when: When you need to «read everything, find the essential, formulate conclusions».
sc-research.impact: With design:research-synthesis — you get a report at the level of a UX researcher.
sc-research.example: Here are 12 interview transcripts — find 5 key themes and prioritize the problems.
sc-research.mistakes: Asking for a «market overview» without criteria and format — you'll get fluff.

sc-data.title: Data analysis
sc-data.what: CSV / XLSX / JSON / SQL dumps — Claude reads, computes aggregates, looks for anomalies, plots charts. Especially strong with Code execution: real numbers, not approximations.
sc-data.why: To move from Excel formulas to human language: «find top-5 SKUs with revenue drops and explain the pattern» — without VLOOKUP.
sc-data.when: When there's a data table and questions like «what's interesting here», «what's anomalous», «what are the trends».
sc-data.impact: Removes the «tool tax»: instead of an hour on formulas — minutes of conversation with the data.
sc-data.example: Upload a CSV of orders → «Find SKUs with a >30% drop in March vs February. Show top-5 with possible causes from available columns».
sc-data.mistakes: Asking to «analyze the data» without a question — you'll get a generic description. Good analysis starts from a concrete question.

b-educators.title: Claude for educators
b-educators.what: Claude handles the preparation routine: lesson plans, explanations at different levels, assignments, quizzes, feedback — freeing time for real interaction with students.
b-educators.why: Educators spend up to 40% of their working time preparing materials. Claude cuts that time 3–5× without sacrificing quality.
b-educators.when: When planning a lesson, developing differentiated tasks, writing personalised feedback, or explaining complex concepts at multiple levels.
b-educators.impact: 5–10 hours saved per week; more differentiated materials; the teacher focuses on pedagogical judgment rather than routine text.
b-educators.example: «Explain photosynthesis in three ways: for a 6-year-old, a 12-year-old, and a biology undergraduate» — three ready explanations in seconds.
b-educators.mistakes: Letting Claude evaluate all student work without review — the teacher's pedagogical judgment is irreplaceable; Claude only speeds up the draft feedback.

agents.title: Agent ideas
agents.what: Ready-made Subagent templates for routines: reviewer, auditor, researcher, technical writer, manager assistant.
agents.why: To turn a repeating process into a button — without manual prompting every time.
agents.when: When you catch yourself thinking «I'm explaining the same thing again».
agents.impact: A good agent = -80% time on a typical task.
agents.example: Create a Subagent for your regular task: description, role, report template, and trigger by keywords.
agents.mistakes: Building an agent for a task that occurs once a month — no payoff.

ag-principles.title: Agent design principles
ag-principles.what: A good agent: narrow purpose, clear trigger, limited tool set, explicit fallback paths, observability (logs / metrics), idempotency for dangerous actions. Without these 6 properties an agent is just a long prompt.
ag-principles.why: Most «non-working» agents fail on one of these. Principles are a checklist before launch, not «best practices» after the fact.
ag-principles.when: Before creating any agent — walk through the principles as a filter. If on 2+ points you «didn't think about it» — the agent isn't ready.
ag-principles.impact: Design by principles = 3-5× fewer «weird behaviors» in prod; easier to debug, easier to hand off to the team.
ag-principles.example: Trigger: «review PR». Tools: only git diff + Read. Fallback: if diff > 1000 lines — ask the user to narrow scope. Observability: log to .claude/logs/code-reviewer.jsonl.
ag-principles.mistakes: Giving the agent 30 tools «just in case» — it'll pick the wrong ones. A narrow surface = more reliable.

ag-code.title: Code Reviewer
ag-code.what: An agent that checks PRs/commits against a checklist: security, readability, tests, regressions.
ag-code.why: Lifts the pre-review routine off a human — they see the already filtered stuff.
ag-code.when: In every repository with a PR process.
ag-code.impact: Review quality grows, expert time saves multifold.
ag-code.example: Subagent code-reviewer: trigger «review PR», output — list of comments by severity.
ag-code.mistakes: Trusting only the agent — doesn't replace the expert's architectural thinking.

ag-ux.title: Audit Agent
ag-ux.what: An agent takes input material and produces an audit by fixed criteria.
ag-ux.why: Needed everywhere there are regular releases and a pre-release check.
ag-ux.when: When there's no time for a manual full audit but you need a signal «is it okay?».
ag-ux.impact: Ideal paired with an MCP server to the relevant system and topical Skills.
ag-ux.example: Agent auditor: input — material, output — top-N problems sorted by impact.
ag-ux.mistakes: Replacing checks with real users by this — the agent has hypotheses, people have facts.

ag-research.title: Researcher
ag-research.what: An agent searches sources, synthesizes, delivers a report with references — for marketing or product.
ag-research.why: Removes 70% of the «dirty» work: reading, note-taking, citing.
ag-research.when: Before a product launch, in competitor analysis, market overview.
ag-research.impact: With Web search + a topical Skill — delivers quality of a competent analyst.
ag-research.example: Agent researcher: topic + 3 questions → 2-page report with sources and a comparison table.
ag-research.mistakes: Accepting conclusions without verifying sources — the model can hallucinate links.

ag-designer.title: Designer Assistant
ag-designer.what: An on-demand agent: design critique, UX copy, component variants, accessibility check.
ag-designer.why: A discussion partner — asks questions, suggests alternatives, catches flaws.
ag-designer.when: In a design team during research and iteration — before handoff.
ag-designer.impact: Replaces the «second pair of eyes» when a colleague is busy, plus faster.
ag-designer.example: Agent designer-buddy: input — layout / URL → 5 observations + 3 alternative ideas.
ag-designer.mistakes: Expecting flawless artistic taste from it — it's strong in heuristics, not aesthetics.

ag-pm.title: PM Assistant
ag-pm.what: An agent writes user stories, formulates acceptance criteria, breaks down tasks, prepares standup updates.
ag-pm.why: Frees the PM from formulation routine — leaves time for strategy.
ag-pm.when: In product teams with an active backlog and sprints.
ag-pm.impact: Less misalignment with the team — tasks are clear and uniform.
ag-pm.example: Agent pm-assistant: task statement → User story + AC + risks + size estimate.
ag-pm.mistakes: Replacing stakeholder interviews with generation — hypotheses ≠ user needs.

cap-thinking.title: Extended Thinking
cap-thinking.what: Claude reasons step-by-step in a hidden thinking block before answering. The model explores approaches, checks itself, and only then forms the final response. Available on Opus and Sonnet via API.
cap-thinking.why: Hard problems (math, logic, multi-step planning) solved much better with explicit internal reasoning.
cap-thinking.when: Complex analysis, multi-step proofs, architectural decisions, debugging tricky bugs, strategy planning.
cap-thinking.impact: Significantly higher accuracy on hard tasks. The thinking block is visible — you can inspect the reasoning chain.
cap-thinking.example: Send a prompt with thinking enabled: Claude explores approaches in the thinking block, picks the best, then delivers the answer.
cap-thinking.mistakes: Enabling thinking for simple tasks — wastes tokens and adds latency with no benefit.

ag-managed.title: Claude Managed Agents
ag-managed.what: Official Anthropic product: a ready-made, configurable agent harness that runs in managed cloud infrastructure. Handles long-running tasks asynchronously — you submit a task, the agent runs, you poll for results.
ag-managed.why: Building a reliable agent loop from scratch (retries, timeouts, state, observability) takes weeks. Managed Agents provides this out of the box.
ag-managed.when: Long-running tasks (minutes to hours), asynchronous work, production agent deployments that need reliability and scalability.
ag-managed.impact: Cuts agent infrastructure work from weeks to hours. Production-grade reliability without custom DevOps.
ag-managed.example: Submit a task: "research this topic and write a report". Managed Agent runs, uses web search and file tools, returns structured results when done.
ag-managed.mistakes: Using Managed Agents for simple single-turn tasks — overkill. Use the Messages API directly for those.

cc-grp-session.title: Session management
cc-grp-session.what: /clear — new session. /compact — summarize context to free space. /resume — continue a previous session. /rename — name the current conversation. /background — keep running after terminal closes. /branch — fork conversation at current point. /rewind — restore code and chat to earlier state. /export — save conversation to file. /copy — copy last response. /recap — one-line session summary. /desktop — move to Claude Desktop. /teleport — resume from claude.ai. /remote-control — control session from phone. /exit — close CLI.
cc-grp-session.why: Sessions are persistent — you can pause, resume, fork, and export any conversation. Understanding session commands prevents losing context.
cc-grp-session.when: Long coding sessions, switching devices, saving progress, recovering from mistakes with /rewind.
cc-grp-session.impact: Never lose work. Resume complex multi-hour tasks. Fork experiments without breaking the main session.
cc-grp-session.example: /branch before a risky refactor → experiment freely → if it fails, original session intact.
cc-grp-session.mistakes: Using /clear when you meant /compact — /clear deletes context, /compact summarizes it.

cc-grp-context.title: Context and code
cc-grp-context.what: /add-dir — add a directory to Claude's working context. /context — visualize current context usage as a grid. /memory — edit CLAUDE.md memory files. /diff — view uncommitted changes and per-turn diffs. /focus — show only prompt, tool summary, and final response. /goal — set a goal and keep working until condition met. /init — generate CLAUDE.md for current project.
cc-grp-context.why: Claude's context window is finite. These commands let you control what Claude sees and focus its attention.
cc-grp-context.when: Large codebases (add only relevant dirs), long sessions (monitor with /context), starting new projects (/init).
cc-grp-context.impact: Better answers, fewer hallucinations, faster responses — Claude sees exactly what it needs.
cc-grp-context.example: /add-dir src/components → Claude now reads all component files without you referencing each one.
cc-grp-context.mistakes: Adding the entire repo when only one folder is relevant — wastes context and slows Claude down.

cc-grp-model.title: Model and limits
cc-grp-model.what: /model — switch the AI model for current session. /fast — toggle fast mode (uses Haiku). /effort — set effort level for model usage. /advisor — consult a stronger model at key moments. /upgrade — upgrade to Max for higher limits. /usage — show session cost, plan usage, activity stats. /status — show Claude Code version, model, account, API connectivity. /extra-usage — configure extra usage when limits hit.
cc-grp-model.why: Different tasks need different models. Switching mid-session saves cost without losing context.
cc-grp-model.when: Use /fast for quick edits, /model for architecture work, /usage to track spend, /status to diagnose connection issues.
cc-grp-model.impact: Significant cost savings. Correct model for each task. Never hit limits unexpectedly.
cc-grp-model.example: /fast for writing tests → /model Opus for the tricky algorithm → back to /fast for cleanup.
cc-grp-model.mistakes: Never checking /usage — unexpected bill at end of month.

cc-grp-ui.title: Interface and appearance
cc-grp-ui.what: /color — set prompt bar color for this session. /theme — change the overall theme. /tui — set terminal UI renderer (default or fullscreen). /terminal-setup — enable Option+Enter for newlines and visual bell. /voice — toggle voice mode. /focus — show minimal output (prompt + summary + response only). /radio — Claude FM lo-fi background music. /stickers — order physical Claude Code stickers.
cc-grp-ui.why: A comfortable interface reduces friction during long coding sessions.
cc-grp-ui.when: /theme and /color for visual clarity. /terminal-setup once after install. /focus when output is too noisy.
cc-grp-ui.impact: Less cognitive load. Better readability in long sessions.
cc-grp-ui.example: /theme dark + /color #d97757 → visually distinct Claude terminal from other windows.
cc-grp-ui.mistakes: Skipping /terminal-setup — Option+Enter won't work for multi-line prompts on macOS.

cc-grp-config.title: Configuration and settings
cc-grp-config.what: /config — open the config panel. /keybindings — open or create keybindings config file. /permissions — manage allow and deny tool permission rules. /privacy-settings — view and update privacy settings. /update-config — configure settings.json via natural language. /sandbox — configure sandbox for tool execution. /remote-env — configure default remote environment.
cc-grp-config.why: Permissions and keybindings are core to safe, efficient Claude Code usage. Misconfigured permissions = constant approval prompts.
cc-grp-config.when: /permissions after first install to allowlist common tools. /keybindings to set Cmd+Enter as submit. /config for one-stop settings overview.
cc-grp-config.impact: Fewer interruptions, faster workflow, safer execution.
cc-grp-config.example: /permissions → allow 'Bash(npm run *)' → Claude can run npm scripts without asking every time.
cc-grp-config.mistakes: Allowing all bash commands globally — security risk. Be specific: 'Bash(npm run *)' not 'Bash(*)'.

cc-grp-integrations.title: Integrations
cc-grp-integrations.what: /mcp — manage MCP servers (add, remove, list). /ide — manage IDE integrations (VS Code, JetBrains) and show status. /chrome — Claude in Chrome beta settings. /hooks — view hook configurations for tool events. /plugin — manage Claude Code plugins. /reload-plugins — activate pending plugin changes. /agents — manage agent configurations. /install-github-app — set up Claude GitHub Actions. /install-slack-app — install Claude Slack app. /web-setup — setup Claude Code on the web.
cc-grp-integrations.why: Integrations extend Claude Code into your full development workflow — IDE, GitHub, Slack, browser.
cc-grp-integrations.when: /ide after installing VS Code extension. /mcp to connect databases or APIs. /hooks for pre/post-tool automation.
cc-grp-integrations.impact: Claude works inside your existing tools instead of alongside them.
cc-grp-integrations.example: /ide → VS Code integration active → Claude sees open files and inline diagnostics automatically.
cc-grp-integrations.mistakes: /reload-plugins not called after adding a plugin — new plugin won't activate until next session.

cc-grp-automation.title: Automation and AI tasks
cc-grp-automation.what: /plan — enable plan mode or view current session plan. /autofix-pr — monitor and autofix issues with current PR. /tasks — list and manage background tasks. /loop — run a prompt or command on recurring interval. /schedule — create scheduled remote agent routines. /batch — plan a large-scale change, execute across 5-30 parallel worktree agents. /ultraplan — draft a plan on the web for editing and approval. /ultrareview — deep bug finding ($5-20, runs on web). /goal — set a completion condition and keep working until met. /background — continue session in background.
cc-grp-automation.why: These commands turn Claude from a chat assistant into an autonomous worker that runs tasks while you focus elsewhere.
cc-grp-automation.when: /loop for recurring tasks. /batch for large refactors across many files. /schedule for nightly automation. /ultrareview before major releases.
cc-grp-automation.impact: Hours of work compressed into background tasks. Claude handles parallelism you couldn't manage manually.
cc-grp-automation.example: /batch 'add JSDoc to all functions in src/' → 20 parallel agents, each opens a PR for their file group.
cc-grp-automation.mistakes: Running /batch without /plan first — always approve the plan before parallel execution.

cc-grp-quality.title: Code quality and review
cc-grp-quality.what: /review — review a pull request with structured analysis. /security-review — security review of pending branch changes. /simplify — review changed code for reuse, quality, efficiency. /debug — enable debug logging for session diagnostics. /fewer-permission-prompts — scan transcripts, build allowlist to reduce permission interruptions. /diff — view uncommitted changes and per-turn diffs.
cc-grp-quality.why: These are the quality gates before shipping. Claude catches what linters miss: logic errors, security issues, over-engineering.
cc-grp-quality.when: Before every PR merge: /review. Before deploy: /security-review. After a long session: /simplify.
cc-grp-quality.impact: Fewer bugs in production. Cleaner code. Security issues caught before they ship.
cc-grp-quality.example: /review → Claude lists issues by severity: Critical (SQL injection risk), Warning (no error handling), Info (rename for clarity).
cc-grp-quality.mistakes: Using /review as a rubber stamp — read the output carefully, especially Critical items.

cc-grp-help.title: Help, learning and account
cc-grp-help.what: /help — show all available commands. /powerup — discover Claude Code features through quick interactive lessons. /release-notes — view what's new. /btw — ask a side question without interrupting main task. /insights — analyze your Claude Code session patterns. /skills — list available installed skills. /team-onboarding — generate a guide for teammates. /login / /logout — account management. /feedback — submit feedback to Anthropic. /doctor — diagnose installation issues. /mobile — QR code for mobile app.
cc-grp-help.why: Onboarding and ongoing learning. /btw and /insights are underused gems.
cc-grp-help.when: /doctor when something breaks. /powerup when starting out. /btw for quick questions mid-task. /insights weekly to see your usage patterns.
cc-grp-help.impact: /btw alone saves dozens of context-breaking interruptions per day.
cc-grp-help.example: Mid-refactor: /btw what does the Builder pattern solve? → Claude answers briefly → main task continues.
cc-grp-help.mistakes: Never running /doctor when CLI behaves strangely — it catches 90% of common issues instantly.

pl-cowork.title: Claude Cowork
pl-cowork.what: Agentic task automation built into Claude Desktop (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise). Claude plans multi-step work, breaks it into subtasks, runs code in an isolated VM on your machine, and writes results directly to your file system. Unlike chat, you describe an outcome — Claude handles every step.
pl-cowork.why: Complex knowledge work — file organization, data analysis, document creation — requires many coordinated steps and local file access. Cowork handles this autonomously so you can step away and come back to finished results.
pl-cowork.when: Organizing a chaotic folder, processing hundreds of receipts, synthesizing research from multiple documents, building spreadsheets with formulas, creating reports. NOT for simple questions — use regular chat instead.
pl-cowork.impact: Hours of repetitive file and document work done while you focus on other things. Can run scheduled tasks automatically (daily, weekly) without any code or APIs.
pl-cowork.example: Task: Sort my Downloads folder by type, extract total amounts from all receipt screenshots, create an Excel report with monthly totals. Claude plans the steps, reads files, runs analysis, and saves the finished spreadsheet — all without your involvement.
pl-cowork.mistakes: Using Cowork for simple Q&A — wastes your usage quota significantly. Closing the Desktop app while a task runs — this stops it immediately. Granting access to your entire drive — connect only the folder you need.

pl-integrations.title: Integrations
pl-integrations.what: Claude connects to external apps and platforms via built-in connectors. Key integrations: Chrome extension (reads/navigates/fills forms in your browser, side panel, tab groups, scheduled browser tasks — paid plans, beta). Microsoft 365 (read-only access to Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Word, Excel, PowerPoint — all plans). Google Workspace (Drive, Gmail, Calendar via Plus menu connectors). Slack (search messages, meeting transcripts).
pl-integrations.why: Keeps Claude inside your existing workflow instead of requiring you to copy-paste content between apps. Claude sees the context you're already working in.
pl-integrations.when: Chrome: automating repetitive browser tasks, extracting data from websites, filling forms. M365: asking questions about your emails, documents, meetings without leaving Claude. Google: referencing Drive files or calendar events in chat. Slack: finding past decisions or meeting summaries.
pl-integrations.impact: Eliminates the biggest friction in AI workflows — manually moving context between tools. Claude becomes a layer on top of your existing apps.
pl-integrations.example: Enable M365 connector → ask Claude: 'Summarize the emails from last week about the budget proposal and list open action items.' Claude searches Outlook and Teams, reads the threads, and returns a structured summary.
pl-integrations.mistakes: Expecting M365/Google connectors to take actions (send emails, create docs) — they are READ-ONLY for now. Not granting the necessary permissions when installing Chrome extension — Claude can't see page content without them.

cap-limitations.title: Capabilities & Limitations
cap-limitations.what: Claude is powerful but has real constraints every user must understand. Key limitations: Knowledge cutoff (training data ends ~early 2026, no awareness of events after that). Hallucinations (Claude can confidently state incorrect facts, especially on niche topics or when 'filling gaps'). No real-time data (can't browse the web unless web search is enabled). Context window (long conversations cause earlier content to 'fall out'). No image generation. Literal interpretation (misses sarcasm, cultural nuance, implicit meaning).
cap-limitations.why: Most AI mistakes happen because users don't know the boundaries. Understanding limitations lets you design prompts and workflows that work around them instead of running into them.
cap-limitations.when: Any time you use Claude for factual claims, recent events, long-running tasks, or high-stakes decisions — verify outputs. Never rely solely on Claude for legal, medical, or financial advice.
cap-limitations.impact: Users who understand limitations make 3-5x fewer errors. They verify outputs, use web search when needed, break long tasks into shorter sessions, and treat Claude as a first draft rather than a final source.
cap-limitations.example: Bad: 'What is the current stock price of Apple?' — Claude will either refuse or hallucinate. Good: Enable web search, or ask Claude to reason from what it knows and flag what needs verification.
cap-limitations.mistakes: Treating Claude's confident tone as a signal of accuracy — it is not. Assuming Claude knows recent events — its training has a cutoff. Using one long chat for a multi-day project — context degrades. Not verifying facts on critical documents.

pr-4d.title: 4D Framework
pr-4d.what: Anthropic's meta-framework for effective AI collaboration, co-developed with Ringling College and University College Cork. Four skills that apply to every AI interaction regardless of model or tool: Delegation (choosing what to give AI), Description (writing clear prompts), Discernment (evaluating output critically), Diligence (iterating until the result is safe and accurate). Defines 24 specific behaviors of effective AI use.
pr-4d.why: Most AI failures happen at one of these four stages, not because of the model. A strong prompt to the wrong task (bad Delegation), a correct task with a vague prompt (bad Description), accepting hallucinated output (bad Discernment), or publishing an unverified first draft (bad Diligence). Fixing the stage fixes the failure.
pr-4d.when: Use as a checklist before every significant AI task: Am I delegating the right work? Is my prompt specific enough? Did I verify the output? Is this iteration ready to use? Takes 30 seconds — saves hours of rework.
pr-4d.impact: Users who internalize the 4D Framework produce reliable AI output consistently. It is transferable across all AI tools — skills do not become obsolete when models change.
pr-4d.example: Delegation: 'This research synthesis is suitable for AI.' Description: 'Summarize these 5 articles into 3 key themes for a non-technical audience, max 200 words each.' Discernment: 'Claude cited a statistic I cannot verify — flag it.' Diligence: 'Revise theme 2 — it misses the regulatory angle from article 3.'
pr-4d.mistakes: Skipping Delegation — giving AI tasks that require human judgment (ethical decisions, relationship-sensitive communications). Skipping Discernment — publishing AI output without fact-checking. Stopping at one iteration — Diligence means feedback loops, not a single send.

foundation.title: Foundation
foundation.what: Core AI components: technologies, tools, concepts. Includes all Claude knowledge (models, context, prompts, Skills, MCP, agents) plus universal AI building blocks (LLM, RAG, Embeddings).
foundation.why: Without understanding the components, you cannot build systems. Foundation is the vocabulary the rest of the map speaks.
foundation.when: When you need to understand how a specific AI tool or concept works.
foundation.impact: Knowing the Foundation, you can evaluate any AI news, choose a stack, argue with a vendor with substance.
foundation.example: What is the context window? — Foundation/Claude-core. What is RAG? — Foundation/AI-fundamentals.
foundation.mistakes: Learning Foundation linearly cover-to-cover is a mistake. Better: go from a task and drill down here as needed.

systems.title: Systems
systems.what: How to connect AI components into working systems. Workflow patterns, orchestration, data systems, human-AI collaboration, AI operations.
systems.why: Knowing what an "agent" is is not enough. You need to know how multiple agents coordinate, how context is passed, how to do quality gates.
systems.when: When the task requires ≥2 AI steps with conditions, humans, tools.
systems.impact: Systems thinking is the shift from "AI experiments" to "AI in production."
systems.example: Multi-agent workflow for customer support: coordinator-agent → routing → specialized subagents.
systems.mistakes: Building a multi-agent system without understanding the basic workflow. Start with a linear chain.

transformation.title: Transformation
transformation.what: How AI changes specific departments and teams: Operations, Marketing, Product, Customer Support. Real workflows with measurable metrics.
transformation.why: Atlas is not a tool encyclopedia. The main value is showing the path from a current process to AI-native operations.
transformation.when: When you need to plan an AI adoption in your team / role / business.
transformation.impact: Knowing the transformation directions, you can justify the AI initiative to leadership with numbers.
transformation.example: AI-Native Operations: reporting automation, decision support, resource optimization — with maturity stages.
transformation.mistakes: Taking AI without integration into the real team workflow leaves it as a PoC. Transformation = workflow + people.

use-cases.title: Use Cases
use-cases.what: Specific named scenarios: "Launch AI tier-1 support", "Deploy AI reporting". Each Use Case is a path through Foundation + Systems + Transformation nodes.
use-cases.why: A Use Case answers "where to start". Not a course, but a map for solving a specific business task.
use-cases.when: When you have a specific goal and need a "route" through Atlas nodes.
use-cases.impact: In 2-4 weeks of working with a Use Case you can move from "we tried AI" to "working workflow in the team".
use-cases.example: uc-ai-reporting-launch: deploying AI reporting in 2 weeks — a path through 5-6 nodes at different levels.
use-cases.mistakes: Using a Use Case as a linear course. It is a map; you can skip nodes you already know.

sys-overview.title: About the Systems layer
sys-overview.what: Entry point to the Systems layer: patterns for connecting AI components into working systems.
sys-overview.why: So users immediately see the layer structure — workflows, orchestration, data, integration, human-AI, ops.
sys-overview.when: On first exposure to the Systems direction.
sys-overview.impact: Understanding that Systems is about HOW, not WHAT.
sys-overview.example: Next, pick a specific sub-direction: AI Workflows / AI Orchestration / etc.
sys-overview.mistakes: Skipping the overview and going straight into details loses the context of the whole layer.

tf-overview.title: About the Transformation layer
tf-overview.what: Entry point to the Transformation layer: 7 directions (Operations, Marketing, Product, Support, Design, Enterprise, eCommerce).
tf-overview.why: So users pick their role / department and go there directly.
tf-overview.when: On first exposure to the Transformation direction.
tf-overview.impact: Understanding that Atlas describes not just Claude, but AI-transformation of real business processes.
tf-overview.example: Next: AI-Native Operations / AI-Native Marketing / AI-Native Customer Support.
tf-overview.mistakes: Thinking Transformation = marketing. It is about real workflows with metrics.

uc-overview.title: What is a Use Case in Atlas
uc-overview.what: A Use Case = a named path through several Atlas nodes for solving a specific business task.
uc-overview.why: To give the user a starting point. Not "learn everything", but "here is a path to your goal".
uc-overview.when: When you have a specific task / goal in a team or product.
uc-overview.impact: Structured workflow instead of chaotic exploration.
uc-overview.example: uc-ai-reporting-launch — a path through 5-6 nodes with an explicit outcome and metrics.
uc-overview.mistakes: Making "your own Use Case" without an explicit outcome and metrics — you get a vague list of links.

ai-fundamentals.title: AI Fundamentals
ai-fundamentals.what: Universal AI concepts not tied to any single model: LLM, embeddings, vector databases, RAG. The vocabulary every AI system speaks — from ChatGPT to your own pipeline on open-source models.
ai-fundamentals.why: Atlas covers Claude in depth, but the AI industry is broader. To talk with engineers, evaluate vendor proposals, and make architectural decisions — you need the common concepts.
ai-fundamentals.when: When reading a technical doc / proposal with AI terms. When choosing a tech stack. When discussing architecture with your team.
ai-fundamentals.impact: Knowing fundamentals shifts you from «I use AI» to «I understand what I am doing». You gain confidence in decisions and substantive arguments.
ai-fundamentals.example: A RAG pipeline uses embeddings (a fundamental concept), stores them in a vector database (a fundamental technology), and feeds relevant chunks into an LLM (a fundamental architecture). Knowing all three — you can read any RAG documentation.
ai-fundamentals.mistakes: Learning fundamentals as abstract theory. More effective: take a concrete task (e.g., «build search over my docs») and learn the needed concepts as you go.

af-llm-basics.title: LLM: How It Works
af-llm-basics.what: Large Language Model — a transformer neural network trained to predict the next token in text. Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama — all LLMs. They differ in size (billions of parameters), architecture (decoder-only, mixture-of-experts), and training data.
af-llm-basics.why: To understand why an LLM errs, hallucinates, or forgets yesterday's conversation — you need to know what is inside. This explains EVERY limitation: context window, cost, latency, hallucinations.
af-llm-basics.when: Before deep AI usage. Before arguing with a developer about «why the model cannot do X». Before estimating cost / latency of infrastructure.
af-llm-basics.impact: Understanding LLMs = understanding the boundaries. Knowing the model does not «think» but statistically predicts — you stop expecting miracles and start designing prompts correctly.
af-llm-basics.example: Prompt: «What is 47×83?» — the LLM predicts token-by-token and may err in one digit. Solution: give it a tool (calculator tool use) or ask for chain-of-thought. This is a direct consequence of the architecture.
af-llm-basics.mistakes: Thinking the LLM «knows» facts. It knows token patterns. Fresh facts, exact numbers, your company specifics — NOT in the LLM. Solution: external sources (RAG, tools).

af-embeddings.title: Embeddings: Vector Representations
af-embeddings.what: An embedding is a representation of text (or image, audio) as a vector of numbers (e.g., 1536 dimensions). Semantically similar texts produce close vectors. This enables search «by meaning», not by exact word match.
af-embeddings.why: Embeddings are the foundation of semantic search, RAG, clustering, recommendations. Without them you cannot build a «smart search» that finds «how to configure the router» from the query «no internet at home».
af-embeddings.when: When you need to search large text volumes by meaning. When building RAG. When you need recommendations (similar products / docs / people).
af-embeddings.impact: Embeddings turn unstructured text into data you can work with mathematically. This is the shift from keyword search to semantic search — quality gain of 30-50%.
af-embeddings.example: The texts «how to reset my password» and «forgot password, please help» — keyword search will not connect them (few common words). Embedding vectors of these phrases will be close → semantic search finds both for «password reset».
af-embeddings.mistakes: Using embeddings from a random model. Search quality depends directly on embedding model quality. OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, Cohere embed-v3, or natively via Claude — the choice matters.

af-vector-db.title: Vector Databases
af-vector-db.what: A database optimized for storing and searching embeddings (vectors). Does what a regular DB cannot: «find the 10 closest vectors to this one». Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector (Postgres extension), Qdrant, Chroma.
af-vector-db.why: Without a vector DB, embeddings are useless: you need to store millions of vectors and quickly find nearest neighbors. A regular DB does this slowly (O(n) scan). A vector DB uses ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF) — search in milliseconds.
af-vector-db.when: RAG systems with >1000 documents. Semantic search over a large knowledge base. Recommendation systems. Anomaly detection.
af-vector-db.impact: A vector DB turns a «search attempt» into a production-ready system: latency <100ms, scale to billions of vectors, metadata filters.
af-vector-db.example: You have 50,000 knowledge base articles. You want a user to ask a question — the system finds the 5 most relevant and feeds them to Claude as context. Without a vector DB — each query takes 30+ seconds. With a vector DB — <100ms.
af-vector-db.mistakes: Choosing a managed solution (Pinecone) when pgvector suffices. Postgres + pgvector is often easier for a team that already knows SQL — and cheaper. Managed is needed at >10M vectors or special requirements.

af-rag-basics.title: RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation
af-rag-basics.what: RAG = feeding the LLM relevant chunks from your knowledge base as context before it generates an answer. Pipeline: query → embedding → vector search → top-K chunks → prompt «Answer based on this context» → LLM.
af-rag-basics.why: The LLM does not know your documents. Without RAG, it either hallucinates or says «I do not know». With RAG — it answers from your data with source citations. This is the most common production AI pattern.
af-rag-basics.when: Chatbots over corporate knowledge bases. Search with AI summaries. Customer support with automated answers. Analysis of large document sets.
af-rag-basics.impact: Transforms the LLM from a «generative helper» into an «expert on your data». Answer accuracy: 30% (without RAG) → 85%+ (with well-built RAG).
af-rag-basics.example: Query: «What is our return policy?». RAG: 1) embedding of query → 2) search in vector DB → 3) find the Returns Policy section → 4) Claude answers based on the finding with a citation. No hallucinations.
af-rag-basics.mistakes: Doing naive RAG: one chunk = one page, retrieval top-3, straight into prompt. Production RAG needs re-ranking, hybrid search (keyword + semantic), chunk overlap, metadata. This is the difference between «kind of works» and «actually works».

af-memory-systems.title: AI Memory: Types
af-memory-systems.what: AI systems have 4 memory types. In-context — what is in the current prompt (short, ephemeral). External — RAG / knowledge base (long-term, selective). Semantic — embeddings of past interactions (search by meaning). Episodic — log of specific events (recover exact sequence).
af-memory-systems.why: Without understanding memory types, you build a chatbot that «does not remember yesterday's conversation» — and you do not know what to do. Each type solves a different problem.
af-memory-systems.when: When designing conversational AI. When users complain «AI forgot what I said». When you need personalization that persists across sessions.
af-memory-systems.impact: Right memory architecture transforms AI from «1-request helper» into «colleague who remembers context». This is the shift from toy demo to production assistant.
af-memory-systems.example: Claude Memory (cap-memory) = semantic memory. Project Files (p-files) = external memory. CLAUDE.md (i-claudemd) = persistent instructions, also a form of external memory. Each has its role.
af-memory-systems.mistakes: Trying to cram all history into context («increase the window to 1M»). Expensive, slow, does not scale. Production solution — combination of types: short-term in-context + long-term external + episodic for important events.

af-multimodal.title: Multimodal AI
af-multimodal.what: AI working with multiple data types simultaneously: text + images + audio + video + code. Claude natively processes text and images. GPT-4 + Gemini add voice. The future — a single model for all modalities.
af-multimodal.why: The real world is multimodal. UX feedback = screenshot + comment. Support = voice call + photo of the problem. Building purely text-based AI systems means ignoring half the context.
af-multimodal.when: When a task requires understanding beyond text. Screenshot → code. Design mockup → HTML. Document photo (PDF) → structured data. Video → automatic summary.
af-multimodal.impact: Multimodal AI expands the task range by 5-10×. Without it, AI = text assistant. With it = universal helper for any media.
af-multimodal.example: Screenshot of error + «why is it like this?» → Claude sees and reads the stack trace. Figma design mockup → «build the HTML» → ready code. This is impossible in text-only models.
af-multimodal.mistakes: Thinking multimodal = «AI understands the image». Understanding is variable: recognizing objects — yes, reading a complex chart — may err, OCR of handwritten text — weaker than specialized OCR. Test on your data types.

af-fine-tuning.title: Fine-tuning vs Prompting
af-fine-tuning.what: Fine-tuning = retraining the model on your data (thousands of examples) — the model literally updates its weights. Prompting = passing instructions in context without changing the model. 95% of business tasks are solved by prompting + few-shot examples + RAG, no fine-tuning needed.
af-fine-tuning.why: Fine-tuning is an expensive (thousands of $) and slow (days/weeks) process. Plus your model becomes «yours» — you cannot upgrade to a new Claude version without redoing the fine-tuning. Prompting is instant, cheap, flexible.
af-fine-tuning.when: Fine-tuning makes sense when: (1) very specific tone-of-voice that does not transfer in a prompt; (2) very narrow domain with thousands of examples; (3) need to reduce latency/cost via a smaller model.
af-fine-tuning.impact: The right choice saves months. Teams often start with «let us fine-tune» and spend a quarter on data collection. The alternative (prompting + RAG) could have launched in a week.
af-fine-tuning.example: Task: «AI replies in our CEO's style». First: 5-shot prompting with examples of CEO emails + system prompt «reply in this style». If after 50 iterations quality still suffers — then fine-tuning. In 80% of cases — prompting is enough.
af-fine-tuning.mistakes: Doing fine-tuning «just in case». It is technical debt: your model is outdated in half a year, the new Claude version is better than your fine-tuned one. Exhaust prompting + RAG + tools first — only then fine-tuning.
